Let \( A_1, A_2, A_3, \ldots \) be a sequence of finite nonempty sets of positive integers. Given that \( |A_i \cap A_j| = \gcd(i, j) \) for all (not necessarily distinct) positive integers \( i \) and \( j \), compute the minimum possible value of

\[
\sum_{d|250} \max A_d,
\]

where the sum ranges over all positive integer divisors \( d \) of 250.

(For a finite nonempty set \( S \), we define \( \max S \) as the largest element of \( S \).)

Let

\[
M_n=\max A_n.
\]

From the condition with \(i=j=n\),

\[
|A_n|=|A_n\cap A_n|=\gcd(n,n)=n,
\]

so \(A_n\) has exactly \(n\) elements. Hence

\[
M_n\ge n.
\]

Also, for any positive integers \(i,j\),

\[
|A_i\cup A_j|
=|A_i|+|A_j|-|A_i\cap A_j|
=i+j-\gcd(i,j).
\]

Every element of \(A_i\cup A_j\) is at most \(\max(M_i,M_j)\), so

\[
\max(M_i,M_j)\ge i+j-\gcd(i,j).
\]

We now use this for three pairs of divisors of \(250\).

- For \(i=2,\ j=5\):

\[
|A_2\cup A_5|=2+5-1=6,
\]

so \(\max(M_2,M_5)\ge 6\). Since \(M_2\ge 2\) and \(M_5\ge 5\), this forces

\[
M_2+M_5\ge 2+6=8.
\]

- For \(i=10,\ j=25\):

\[
|A_{10}\cup A_{25}|=10+25-5=30,
\]

so \(\max(M_{10},M_{25})\ge 30\). Since \(M_{10}\ge 10\) and \(M_{25}\ge 25\),

\[
M_{10}+M_{25}\ge 10+30=40.
\]

- For \(i=50,\ j=125\):

\[
|A_{50}\cup A_{125}|=50+125-25=150,
\]

so \(\max(M_{50},M_{125})\ge 150\). Since \(M_{50}\ge 50\) and \(M_{125}\ge 125\),

\[
M_{50}+M_{125}\ge 50+150=200.
\]

Also \(M_1\ge 1\) and \(M_{250}\ge 250\). The divisors of \(250\) are

\[
1,2,5,10,25,50,125,250,
\]

so

\[
\sum_{d\mid 250} M_d
\ge 1+(M_2+M_5)+(M_{10}+M_{25})+(M_{50}+M_{125})+250
\]

\[
\ge 1+8+40+200+250=499.
\]

Thus the desired sum is at least \(499\).

It remains to show that \(499\) is attainable. For each positive integer \(m\), choose a finite set \(B_m\) of positive integers such that \(|B_m|=\varphi(m)\), where \(\varphi\) is Euler’s totient function, and make all the sets \(B_m\) pairwise disjoint. For the divisors of \(250\), choose their labels as follows:

\[
\begin{aligned}
B_1&=\{1\},\\
B_2&=\{2\},\\
B_5&=\{3,4,5,6\},\\
B_{10}&=\{7,8,9,10\},\\
B_{25}&=\{11,12,\dots,30\},\\
B_{50}&=\{31,32,\dots,50\},\\
B_{125}&=\{51,52,\dots,150\},\\
B_{250}&=\{151,152,\dots,250\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

For all other \(m\), choose the \(B_m\)’s to be pairwise disjoint sets of positive integers larger than \(250\).

Now define

\[
A_n=\bigcup_{m\mid n} B_m.
\]

Because

\[
\sum_{m\mid n}\varphi(m)=n,
\]

we have \(|A_n|=n\). Also, since the sets \(B_m\) are disjoint,

\[
A_i\cap A_j=\bigcup_{m\mid \gcd(i,j)}B_m,
\]

so

\[
|A_i\cap A_j|=\sum_{m\mid \gcd(i,j)}\varphi(m)=\gcd(i,j).
\]

Thus this gives a valid sequence.

For \(d\mid 250\), the maximum element of \(A_d\) is the largest label appearing in the relevant \(B_m\)’s:

\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccccc}
d&1&2&5&10&25&50&125&250\\ \hline
M_d&1&2&6&10&30&50&150&250
\end{array}
\]

Therefore

\[
\sum_{d\mid 250} M_d
=1+2+6+10+30+50+150+250
=499.
\]

Hence the minimum possible value is

\[
\boxed{499}.
\]
